reasoning:
Both submissions emit identical object code: at the "no legal moves" junction in movegen.inc they replace `call moverInCheck` with `call inCheckSide`, immediately after `ld a,(sideToMove)` loads the side to move into A. The surrounding logic (`or a` / `jr z,utStale`) is untouched, so the routine's return convention (nonzero = in check) is preserved and only the *subject* of the check test changes. That is exactly the fault described: the report states the zero-legal-move detection itself is correct (PERFT passes, mated positions genuinely have zero moves), so the defect must be in the mate-vs-stalemate discrimination, and testing the wrong side explains every observed symptom at once — a side that has just moved legally is by definition not in check, so the test always returned false and every terminal position was filed as a stalemate. It also explains the two passing controls: genuine stalemates still land on `utStale` (correct answer for the wrong reason before, right reason after), and positions with legal replies never reach this branch at all. Neither fix touches search, eval, or the draw rules, so the "also observed" clean areas stay clean.

Correctness_risk is genuinely tied at 4 and I am not manufacturing a split: the assembled bytes are the same, so any residual risk is shared — namely that the diff does not itself show `inCheckSide`'s definition, so a reviewer must confirm that it exists, consumes the side in A, returns the flag in A, and does not clobber anything the caller needs (only A matters here, and A is reloaded on the next line). Neither reaches 5 because that verification is off-diff. The one asymmetry I could find is trivial: Y's comment contains a non-ASCII em dash and its continuation lines sit at column 2 rather than aligned with the code — harmless in sjasmplus/pasmo/z80asm (a leading space keeps them out of the label column), not enough to move the score.

The separation is on the other two axes. X is maximally tight — a single changed line with a short comment stating the intended semantics — so it earns 5 on minimality, but its comment only asserts what the new call does and leaves a reviewer to go read `moverInCheck` to learn why the old call was wrong; that is a 3 on clarity. Y adds four comment lines that name the precise trap: `moverInCheck` ignores A and tests `sideToMove^8`, i.e. the side that just moved, which a legal move never leaves in check. That converts the fix from "trust me" into a falsifiable claim a reviewer can check in one grep, and it permanently documents a calling-convention hazard (a helper that silently ignores its apparent argument) that is precisely the kind of thing that reintroduces this bug at the next call site. I dock Y one point on minimality for being slightly more than the fault strictly requires and for the ragged indentation, but per the rubric the extra scope is warranted rather than sprawl — it is zero-byte documentation of a non-obvious root cause, not additional behaviour.

Merge Y. There is no correctness or size cost relative to X (the functional payload is byte-identical), and the annotation is the only thing separating them, so the choice is free. I would tidy the comment indentation to match the surrounding column and replace the em dash with a hyphen before committing. Blinding note: the difference in commentary style could invite a theory about the two authoring processes; I did not weight any such theory — the scores above rest on the source text alone.
